analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC fine drug companies that file sham FDA petitions to delay cheaper generic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with bipartisan support in April 2025 and has sat on the Senate calendar without a floor vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes file petitions with the FDA right before a cheaper generic or biosimilar competitor is about to win approval. Even weak petitions can stall approval for months while the FDA reviews them, during which the brand company keeps selling at high prices. This bill makes it an unfair method of competition to file an objectively baseless petition whose real purpose is to delay a competitor, lets the Federal Trade Commission sue the filer, and imposes a fine of up to $50,000 per day the petition was under review — or the brand company's revenue from the drug during that period, if greater.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would buy cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars sooner if sham petitions stopped delaying their approval, and the generic and biosimilar companies that compete with brand-name drugmakers.

how_it_helps.text: Makes a baseless FDA petition filed to interfere with a competing generic or biosimilar application an unfair method of competition that the FTC can sue over [S2][S3].

Sets the penalty at the greater of $50,000 for each calendar day the sham petition was under FDA review, or the filer's revenue from the drug during that review period, so delaying cheaper competition stops paying for itself [S3].

Creates a presumption that a petition is part of a sham series when the Health and Human Services Secretary finds it was filed mainly to delay approval and refers it to the FTC, easing the government's path to enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drugmakers that file petitions to buy time against generic competitors, who would face civil penalties and lawsuits, plus the cost to the FTC of enforcing the new authority.

drawbacks.text: The penalty is steep enough that some companies may hold back petitions that raise genuine safety or quality concerns, because the line between a legitimate petition and a delaying one is not always clear [S3].
Enforcement depends on the FTC choosing to bring cases and on the HHS Secretary making delay findings, so the deterrent only works as well as those agencies choose to use it [S2][S3].
The bill targets petitions aimed at generic and biosimilar competitors, leaving other ways of slowing competitor entry untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a real one: sham petitions have been a documented way to keep cheaper drugs off the market, and a financial penalty that scales with the delay directly removes the payoff from filing one. The honest cost is a possible chilling effect on good-faith safety petitions, though the bill attempts to draw the line at petitions that are objectively baseless and aimed at interfering with a competitor rather than at the outcome of FDA review. On balance, the design targets the abuse narrowly and preserves legitimate petitions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill won bipartisan approval in the Senate Judiciary Committee, was reported to the floor, and has been waiting on the Senate calendar without a vote since April 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on March 24, 2025, joined by original cosponsors Senators Grassley, Durbin, Blumenthal, Cruz, Welch, and Booker [S1][S3].

The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered it reported favorably without amendment on April 3, and it was reported and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 45 on April 10, 2025 [S5].
No floor vote has been scheduled since it was placed on the calendar [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers, whose petitions continue to delay generic competition with no penalty, are better off with the bill waiting on the calendar than with it on the floor; patients and generic competitors keep waiting for the savings the bill targets.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction with six bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (IA), Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and reported it out of committee without amendment on April 10, 2025.

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, one of two Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 4 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Senators Durbin, Blumenthal, Welch, and Booker).

against.name: Senate Majority Leader John Thune
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill up for a Senate floor vote since it was placed on the calendar in April 2025.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Has a long record of lobbying against legislation penalizing citizen petitions, which its members use to delay generic competitors' FDA approvals.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced with four Democrats and two Republicans as original cosponsors, and the Republican chairman of the Judiciary Committee reported it favorably without amendment; the lack of floor time is the obstacle, not a party split on the record so far.

industries.note: These companies file FDA citizen petitions that can delay generic and biosimilar approval for months while they keep selling at brand-name prices. The bill removes that payoff with fines of up to $50,000 per day under review or the filer's drug revenue during the delay.
Fewer sham petitions means their applications reach approval faster, letting them enter the market and compete sooner. Their gain is the same thing patients gain: cheaper drugs arriving earlier.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report, which puts it in a strong position on paper, but most Senate bills that reach the calendar without being attached to a larger package never get floor time. A realistic path is passage only if leaders fold it into a broader health or drug-pricing package; otherwise it likely waits on the calendar until the Congress ends.
